stimulus.text:
“The first question that presents itself on the subject is, whether a confederated government be the best for the United States or not? Or in other words, whether the thirteen United States should be reduced to one great republic, governed by one legislature, and under the direction of one executive and judicial; or whether they should continue thirteen confederated republics, under the direction and controul of a supreme federal head for certain defined national purposes only? . . . This government is to possess absolute and uncontroulable power, legislative, executive and judicial, with respect to every object to which it extends, for by the last clause of section 8th, article 1st, it is declared ‘that the Congress shall have power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers.’”

—Brutus, No. 1, New-York Journal, October 18, 1787

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification, C. Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Adoption of the Bill of Rights

stem: Brutus and Madison, in Federalist No. 10, both wrote about a large republic. How did their arguments differ?

options.text: Both agreed a large republic would protect liberty
options.misconception: Madison argued a large republic controls faction; Brutus argued it destroys liberty, so they disagreed.

options.text: Madison argued a large republic controls faction, while Brutus argued it would destroy liberty
Both agreed a large republic would destroy liberty
options.misconception: Madison defended the large republic; only Brutus said it would destroy liberty.

options.text: Madison argued for a small republic, while Brutus argued for a large one
options.misconception: Madison defended the large extended republic, and Brutus wanted small confederated republics, the reverse.

rationales.B: Background from the books: Madison held that extending the sphere takes in more interests and keeps any one faction from dominating, while Brutus held that one great republic would swallow the states and end liberty.
rationales.A: Brutus did not agree; he warned a large republic would end liberty.
rationales.C: Background: Madison defended the large republic; he did not say it would destroy liberty.
rationales.D: Background: Madison backed the large republic, while Brutus backed the small confederated ones.
rationales.general:
1. Background: Madison's claim in Federalist No. 10 was that a wider sphere takes in more parties and interests, so no single faction can dominate.
2. Brutus's claim: one great republic governed by one legislature ends the confederation.
3. Both men start from the same worry, the abuse of power.
4. They split on the cure: Madison trusts size, Brutus trusts small republics close to the people.
Remember: when two writers answer one question, the split is the argument.
